why.en: Followed by the noun phrase the lake, expressing place.
why.kk: Одан кейін мекенді білдіретін the lake тіркесі келеді.
why.ru: За ним идёт именная группа the lake, выражающая место.

items.s: It was the final [[round]] of the competition.

why.en: After the final; plural rounds is possible.
why.kk: the final тіркесінен кейін; көпше rounds түрі мүмкін.
why.ru: После the final; возможно множественное rounds.

why.en: That is the whole subject; no noun follows.
why.kk: That — тұтас бастауыш; одан кейін зат есім жоқ.
why.ru: That — всё подлежащее; существительного после него нет.

why.en: that introduces a content clause: a subordinator.
why.kk: that толықтауыш бағыныңқы сөйлемді ашады: сабақтастырғыш.
why.ru: that вводит изъяснительное придаточное: подчинитель.

why.en: That introduces the noun idea.
why.kk: That idea зат есімін ашады.
why.ru: That вводит существительное idea.

why.en: does is the only verb here and means 'practises'.
why.kk: does — мұндағы жалғыз етістік, «шұғылданады» мағынасында.
why.ru: does — единственный глагол здесь, в значении «занимается».

why.en: do-support for the negative of like.
why.kk: like етістігінің болымсыз түрін жасайтын do көмегі.
why.ru: Вспомогательное do для отрицания при like.

why.en: Modifies the verb arrived: a flat adverb.
why.kk: arrived етістігін анықтайды: сын есіммен тұлғалас үстеу.
why.ru: Относится к глаголу arrived: наречие, совпадающее по форме с прилагательным.

why.en: Between a and a noun; later is possible.
why.kk: a мен зат есімнің арасында; later деуге болады.
why.ru: Между a и существительным; возможно later.

why.en: Stands outside the clause and expresses surprise.
why.kk: Сөйлемнен тыс тұрып, таңданысты білдіреді.
why.ru: Стоит вне предложения и выражает удивление.

why.en: Followed by the noun phrase March: a preposition.
why.kk: Одан кейін March зат есімді тіркесі келеді: предлог.
why.ru: За ним идёт именная группа March: предлог.

items.s: [[Since]] you're here, let's start the meeting.

why.en: Introduces a clause of reason: a subordinating conjunction in this course's terms (a preposition with a clause complement in the Cambridge Grammar, Unit 15).
why.kk: Себеп бағыныңқы сөйлемін ашады: бұл курс бойынша сабақтастырғыш жалғаулық (Cambridge Grammar бойынша сөйлемді алатын предлог, 15-бөлім).
why.ru: Вводит придаточное причины: в терминах этого курса подчинительный союз (в Cambridge Grammar — предлог с придаточным, раздел 15).

title.en: Write the form that the sentence needs

instr.en: Type the form of the word that the sentence needs: a noun, verb, adjective or adverb.
instr.kk: Сөйлемге қажет сөз формасын жазыңыз: зат есім, етістік, сын есім немесе үстеу.
instr.ru: Впишите нужную форму слова: существительное, глагол, прилагательное или наречие.

why.en: After your: a noun; help is both noun and verb (conversion).
why.kk: your сөзінен кейін: зат есім; help әрі зат есім, әрі етістік (конверсия).
why.ru: После your: существительное; help — и существительное, и глагол (конверсия).

why.en: After very, describing the subject: adjective with -ful.
why.kk: very сөзінен кейін бастауышты сипаттайды: -ful жұрнақты сын есім.
why.ru: После very описывает подлежащее: прилагательное с -ful.

why.en: Describes how she explained: adverb.
why.kk: Оның қалай түсіндіргенін сипаттайды: үстеу.
why.ru: Описывает, как она объясняла: наречие.

items.s: The ___ of the new library took two years.

why.en: After The, before of: a noun; here the -ing noun building.
why.kk: The артиклінен кейін, of алдында: зат есім; мұнда -ing зат есімі building.
why.ru: После The, перед of: существительное; здесь это существительное на -ing building.

items.s: Could you ___ the problem a little?

why.en: After Could you: a verb, formed with -ify.
why.kk: Could you тіркесінен кейін: -ify жұрнағымен жасалған етістік.
why.ru: После Could you: глагол с суффиксом -ify.

why.en: The people who experienced the feeling: -ed form.
why.kk: Сезімді бастан кешірген адамдар: -ed формасы.
why.ru: Люди, которые испытали чувство: форма на -ed.

instr.en: Describe a place that matters to you in 100–150 words. Then choose five words and write the class and evidence for each in brackets.
instr.kk: Өзіңізге маңызды бір жерді 100–150 сөзбен сипаттаңыз. Содан кейін бес сөзді таңдап, әрқайсысының сөз табы мен дәлелін жақша ішінде жазыңыз.
instr.ru: Опишите важное для вас место в 100–150 словах. Затем выберите пять слов и укажите в скобках часть речи и доказательство для каждого.

checklist: I used at least one noun as a modifier (a city park).
I used at least one linking verb + adjective.
I used a frequency adverb in mid position.
I used one word in two different classes.
Each annotation gives evidence, not only a label.
acts.model: Model extract: My favourite place is a small city [noun as modifier: cannot take very] park near my flat. It looks [linking verb] peaceful [adjective after a linking verb] in the morning, and I usually [adverb, mid position before the main verb] walk there before work. Locals park [verb: follows the subject, could be parked] their bikes by the gate, while the park [noun: after the] itself stays quiet.

CASES.title: The Mislabelled Archive
CASES.brief:
Welcome to the Bureau. Last night's fault did not only damage words; it damaged the labels. The Records Office catalogues every document by the word classes it contains, and half of those labels are now wrong.

Before I send you into the districts, I need to know you can do what the machine could not: decide a word's class from the evidence in its sentence, not from the word alone.
CASES.debrief:
You have shown the Bureau's first principle: a word's class belongs to its use in a sentence. Work, light, clean and fast changed class from sentence to sentence, and you decided each one from position, form and the words around it.

You also separated class from function: stone in a stone wall is a noun doing a modifier's job. Every later case depends on this distinction.

stages.title: Relabel the drawers
stages.intro: Each card shows a word and the sentence it was filed with. Put it in the drawer for its class in that sentence. Drag the card or tap a drawer.
stages.learned: The same spelling can be a noun, verb, adjective or adverb. Position and possible endings, not the word itself, decide.

items.why: After the determiner her, heading the subject noun phrase.
After very and the linking verb is; lighter is possible.
After you in a question with could, taking the object the fire.
It tells us how she types: it modifies the verb.
A complement after is, describing the subject.
After the subject, with the object the office.
It modifies the verb arrived: a flat adverb with the same form as the adjective.

stages.task: Put each word in the drawer for its class in this sentence.
stages.tip: The same word can belong to different classes in different sentences.

stages.title: Find the verbs in the night report
stages.intro: The night guard's report lost all its verb labels. Find every verb, including auxiliaries. Some words that look like verbs are being used as nouns.
stages.trap: Not a verb here. Check what comes before it: a determiner or adjective means a noun.
stages.learned: A verb follows the subject or an auxiliary and can change for tense. A determiner in front signals a noun, even for words like work and walk.

items.text: The guard {finished} his {walk} at midnight. The lights {were} off, but the {work} on the third floor {had} not {stopped}. Someone {was} {moving} boxes.

notes.finished: past tense after the subject The guard.
notes.were: be as a linking verb in the past.

traps.walk: walk follows his: here it is a noun.
traps.work: work follows the and heads a noun phrase: a noun here.
traps.lights: lights follows The and is plural: a noun.

items.why: The verbs carry tense or follow an auxiliary. walk and work were the traps: they follow his and the.

stages.task: Find all the verbs in the report, including auxiliaries.
stages.tip: Some words that look like verbs are nouns here.

stages.title: Class or function?
stages.intro: The machine labelled every modifier before a noun as an adjective. Decide the true class, then choose the evidence that proves it.
stages.learned: A noun can function as a modifier without becoming an adjective. Adjectives accept very and can follow seem; nouns as modifiers cannot.

evidence: *a very stone bridge and *the bridge seems stone are impossible
items.why: Adjective tests fail, so stone remains a noun functioning as a modifier.

evidence: a very narrow bridge / the bridge seems narrow / narrower
*a very city council is impossible; the city can stand alone as a noun phrase
items.why: city is a noun modifying another noun.

evidence: a very noisy meeting / the meeting seems noisy
It comes first in the phrase
items.why: The ending -y is only a clue; the tests are the proof.

evidence: It follows a brilliant and can be plural: performances
items.why: Meaning (an action) would mislead you; position and form show a noun.

evidence: It follows the determiner Their and heads the subject
items.why: Many nouns name actions. The evidence is grammatical, not semantic.

stages.task: Choose the class of the highlighted word. Then choose the evidence.
stages.tip: A word before a noun is not always an adjective.

stages.title: Training the new archivist
stages.intro: The junior archivist, Timur, has questions about the labels. Choose the reply that gives him a reliable principle.
stages.learned: Meaning is a starting point; form and distribution are the decisive evidence.

lines: Arrival is an action, so it's a verb, right?

options.t: Not here. It follows a determiner and can be plural, so it is a noun.
options.reply: So I should check the grammar around it, not just the meaning. Got it.
options.why: Correct: meaning alone misleads; distribution and form decide.

options.t: Yes. Words for actions are always verbs.
options.reply: Then why does the label say the arrival? Verbs don't follow the.
options.why: Many nouns denote actions: arrival, decision, destruction.

options.t: It depends on how long the word is.
options.reply: Length? That can't be how grammarians decide.
options.why: Word length has nothing to do with word class.

lines: Friendly ends in -ly. Shall I file it with the adverbs?

options.t: No. Test it: a very friendly person, she seems friendly. It modifies a noun, so it is an adjective.
options.reply: So an ending is a clue, not a proof.
options.why: Correct: friendly, lovely, costly are adjectives despite -ly.

options.t: Yes, every -ly word is an adverb.
options.reply: But we write a friendly person. An adverb can't modify person, can it?
options.why: Endings are clues; tests are proof.

options.t: File it under nouns; it names a quality.
options.reply: Then why can it follow very? Nouns can't.
options.why: Nouns do not take very; adjectives do.

lines: Last one: what's the fastest test for whether something is a noun?

options.t: Put the in front and try a plural; then check it heads a phrase that can be a subject.
options.reply: Determiner, plural, subject position. I'll use those three.
options.why: These are standard distributional and morphological tests (Huddleston & Pullum, 2002).

options.t: Ask whether you can touch it.
options.reply: I can't touch happiness, but it's still on the noun shelf.
options.why: Abstract nouns pass the grammatical tests too.

options.t: Check whether it starts with a capital letter.
options.reply: Only proper nouns do that. What about table?
options.why: Capitals mark proper nouns only.

stages.task: Choose the best reply to Timur.
stages.tip: The best reply gives him a rule he can use every time.

CASES.title: The Lost Property Office
CASES.brief:
Everything that was ever lost in Meridian ends up on my shelves. The fault scrambled the inventory: plurals are wrong, things that can't be counted have been counted, and I can't tell objects from descriptions.

Help me put the nouns back in order, starting with today's report.
CASES.debrief:
The inventory is clean. You identified nouns by their position after determiners and adjectives, separated count from non-count uses, repaired irregular plurals and genitives, and recognised the jobs noun phrases do in a sentence.

Remember the shelf rule: non-count nouns such as luggage, advice, information never take -s or a/an.

stages.title: Today's inventory
stages.intro: Find every noun in the clerk's notes, including nouns used as modifiers.
stages.trap: Not a noun in this sentence. Ask: could it follow the here and become plural?
stages.learned: Nouns head noun phrases after determiners and adjectives; a noun before another noun is still a noun.

items.text: A {passenger} left a black {umbrella} and two {gloves} on the {train}. The {driver} brought them to the {office} after {lunch}.

traps.them: a pronoun standing for umbrella and gloves.

items.why: Every noun followed a determiner, a number, an adjective or a preposition.

items.text: Someone found a {wallet} with no {money} but a {library} {card} inside. Its {owner} called about her {luggage} and some important {information}.

traps.inside: an adverb (or preposition without a complement) of place.
traps.Someone: an indefinite pronoun: it cannot take the.

items.why: library was the hard one: a noun modifying another noun.

stages.task: Find all the nouns in the clerk's notes.
stages.tip: Nouns used as modifiers count too: a bus ticket.

stages.title: Count or non-count shelf?
stages.intro: Each item is filed with its sentence. Decide whether the noun is used as count or non-count here.
stages.learned: Countability belongs to a use of a noun. coffee is non-count as a substance and count as a cup; advice, luggage, furniture are non-count.

items.ctx: Your luggage is on the second shelf.
items.why: No plural and a singular verb: luggage is.
Here it means cups of coffee, so it is countable.
advice has no plural; one item is a piece of advice.

items.ctx: It was an experience I'll never forget.
items.why: A single event: count use with an.

items.ctx: The furniture was damaged in the move.
items.why: A collective non-count noun; count items are chairs, tables.

stages.task: Decide if the noun is count or non-count in this sentence.

stages.title: Repair the labels
stages.intro: Type the correct form of the noun for each label. Watch for irregular plurals and genitives.
stages.learned: Irregular plurals form a small closed set; genitive 's marks singulars and an apostrophe alone marks regular plurals.

items.s: Found in the staff room: the ___ coats
items.why: Plural genitive of a regular noun: apostrophe after -s.

items.s: Research report: the three ___ for selection
items.why: Greek plural used in academic English.
sheep has the same form in the plural.

stages.task: Type the correct form of the noun.
stages.tip: Watch for irregular plurals and the genitive 's.

stages.title: The clerk's mistakes
stages.intro: A temporary clerk wrote these notes. Find the faulty word in each and choose the repair.
stages.learned: Non-count nouns take no plural; numbers above one require a plural; nouns modifying nouns stay singular.

items.s: A passenger asked for [[informations]] about her bag.
The owner thanked us for our [[advices]].
It was found in the [[shoes]] department.
items.why: A noun modifying another noun is normally singular: the shoe department.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

stages.title: What is the noun phrase doing?
stages.intro: Final shelf. Decide the function of the bold phrase in its sentence.
stages.learned: Noun phrases can be subjects, objects and complements; a noun can also modify another noun.

items.ctx: The owner of the bag is a librarian.
items.why: After the linking verb is, describing the subject.

items.ctx: She left it at the station café.

stages.task: Decide the job of the bold noun phrase in its sentence.

CASES.title: The Anonymous Letters
CASES.brief:
Three letters arrived at the desk overnight, and the fault has made them hard to follow. Every he, she, it and they points somewhere, and if we follow the wrong one, we question the wrong person.

Trace the pronouns, then help me interview a witness without causing confusion.
CASES.debrief:
The letters make sense again. You traced pronouns back to the noun phrases they stand for, chose subject and object forms correctly, used it for things, and removed pronouns that English does not allow.

The key insight: a pronoun replaces a whole noun phrase, and English gender is natural, not grammatical.

stages.title: Trace the references
stages.intro: Each pronoun stands for something earlier in the letter. Tap the noun phrase it refers to.
stages.learned: A pronoun refers to a whole noun phrase; agreement in number and natural gender, and the logic of the text, identify it.

items.text: <<Mrs Abenova>> called <<Mr Daulet>> because [[she]] had lost her key.
items.why: she is feminine and singular, so only Mrs Abenova fits.

items.text: <<The porter>> gave <<the visitors>> a map, but [[they]] still got lost.
items.why: they is plural, so it can only refer to the visitors.

items.text: <<The parcel>> arrived with <<a note>>. Nobody has opened [[it]] yet, but the note was read at once.
items.why: The note was read, so the unopened item is the parcel.

items.text: <<Daniyar>> told <<his sister>> that [[he]] would pay for the repair.
<<The two guards>> blamed <<the manager>>, so [[he]] wrote a formal reply.
items.why: he is singular; the two guards would be they.

items.text: If <<a resident>> loses <<a card>>, [[they]] should report it to the desk.
items.why: Singular they for an unspecified person: the resident reports, not the card.

stages.task: Tap the words that the highlighted pronoun refers to.

stages.title: Interviewing the witness
stages.intro: Mr Sato saw the delivery van. Your questions must be clear: a wrong pronoun form or reference will confuse him.
stages.learned: Subject forms before verbs, object forms after verbs and prepositions; a pronoun needs a clear antecedent.

lines: The driver and his assistant carried two boxes into the hotel.

options.t: What did the assistant look like?
options.reply: Tall, grey coat, carrying a clipboard.
options.why: Repeating the noun avoids ambiguity: he could mean the driver or the assistant.

options.t: What did he look like?
options.reply: Which one? The driver or the assistant?
options.why: Two possible masculine antecedents: the pronoun is ambiguous here.

options.t: What did him look like?
options.why: him is an object form; the subject of look needs he.

lines: Then the van drove off. It was white, quite old.
items.prompt: Confirm the detail about the van:

options.t: So it was an old white van?
options.why: it is the correct pronoun for a thing.

options.t: So he was an old white van?
options.why: English uses it for objects; Russian фургон — он does not transfer.

options.t: So she was old and white?
options.reply: Who? I was talking about the van.
options.why: she refers to a female person; the van needs it.

lines: The receptionist spoke to the driver and me.

options.t: What did she tell you and him?
options.reply: That the delivery was a day early.
options.why: After tell, object forms: you and him.

options.t: What did she tell you and he?
options.why: After a verb, the object form him is needed.

options.t: What did her tell you?
options.reply: Her? Do you mean the receptionist?
options.why: The subject of tell needs she.

lines: The guests looked after themselves while the porters were busy.

options.t: So the guests carried their own bags?
options.why: themselves refers back to the subject the guests.

options.t: So the porters looked after the guests?
options.reply: No, the porters were busy. The guests helped themselves.
options.why: A reflexive pronoun refers to the subject of its own clause.

options.t: So the guests looked after each other's children?
options.reply: I didn't say that. Each other is different.
options.why: themselves is reflexive; each other is reciprocal.

stages.task: Choose the clearest question for the witness.
stages.tip: A wrong pronoun form or reference will confuse him.

stages.title: Edit the inspector's draft
stages.intro: The draft statement has pronoun errors that a translation tool introduced. Find each one and repair it.
stages.learned: English needs a subject even for weather and distance (it), no resumptive pronoun in relative clauses, and it for objects.

items.task: A required word is missing. Tap the word where the gap begins.
items.why: English needs the dummy subject it: It was raining.

items.s: The van, which the driver had parked [[it]] outside, was unlocked.
items.why: which already stands for the van; the extra pronoun is ungrammatical.

items.s: The receptionist checked the parcel and said [[he]] was damaged.
The manager asked my colleague and [[I]] to wait.
The new guard introduced [[hisself]] to the staff.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

stages.title: Restore the summary
stages.intro: The final summary was cut into pieces. Restore each sentence. One piece in some sentences is a decoy that does not belong.
stages.learned: Existential there introduces new information; dummy it fills the subject before a later clause; relative clauses take no extra pronoun.

a: There was a white van outside the hotel
It is important to find the driver
items.why: It anticipates the real subject to find the driver.

a: This is the parcel that we found
items.why: No pronoun after found: that already refers to the parcel.

a: They blamed themselves for the delay
items.why: Reflexive object referring to the subject They.

stages.task: Tap the pieces in the correct order to rebuild each sentence.
stages.tip: One piece may not belong. Leave it out.

CASES.title: The Registry Desk
CASES.brief:
At the Registry, one small word decides everything: a house or the house, few objections or a few. Since the fault, our clerks have been mixing them up, and citizens leave with the wrong documents.

Spend a shift at my desk. Every determiner you choose changes what the citizen understands.
CASES.debrief:
The desk is running again. You chose articles by asking what the listener can identify, matched quantifiers to count and non-count nouns, separated determiners from pronouns, and put combined determiners in their fixed order.

For Kazakh and Russian speakers this is the hardest closed class in English, so this case is worth replaying.

stages.title: A shift at the desk
stages.intro: Citizens come to the desk. Choose what to say. A wrong article or quantifier causes a real misunderstanding.
stages.learned: the = the listener can identify it; a/an = introduced as new; no article for general plural and non-count reference.

lines: I'd like to register my new address.
You need to fill in a form first.
items.prompt: The citizen has filled in the form you gave. You say:

options.t: Please sign the form at the bottom.
options.why: The form is now identifiable to both of you: the.

options.t: Please sign a form at the bottom.
options.why: a suggests a new, unidentified form.

options.t: Please sign form at the bottom.
options.why: A singular count noun needs a determiner.

items.prompt: You tell her about a café she doesn't know:

options.t: There's a café on the corner.
options.why: New information for the listener: a.

options.t: There's the café on the corner.
options.reply: The café? Should I know it?
options.why: the assumes she can already identify it.

options.t: There's café on the corner.
options.why: Singular count noun without a determiner.

lines: Were there many objections to the new car park?
items.prompt: There were three, which is enough to delay it. You say:

options.t: Yes, a few, so the decision may be delayed.
options.reply: I see, so it's not decided yet.
options.why: a few presents the number as some, enough to matter.

options.t: Few, so the decision may be delayed.
options.why: few without a means almost none, which contradicts the delay.

options.t: Yes, much objections.
options.why: much goes with non-count nouns; objections is plural count.

lines: Do I need any documents for my passport?
items.prompt: He needs some, and you have one sheet of guidance:

options.t: Yes, some documents. Here's some information about them.
options.why: some with plural count and with non-count nouns.

options.t: Yes, some documents. Here's an information about them.
options.why: information is non-count: no an.

options.t: Yes, many document. Here's information sheet.
options.why: many needs a plural; information sheet needs a determiner.

stages.task: Choose what to say to each visitor.
stages.tip: A wrong article or quantifier changes the meaning.

stages.title: Quantity checks
stages.intro: The quantity column was scrambled. Which word fits each noun in its sentence: much, many, or a quantifier that works with both kinds of noun?
stages.learned: much with non-count, many with plural count, and quantifiers such as a lot of, some, no with both.

items.ctx: We don't have ___ time before closing.
Which quantifier works with both money and forms?
items.why: a lot of combines with non-count and plural count nouns.

items.ctx: Which quantifier works with both advice and questions?
How ___ furniture is in the storeroom?

stages.task: Choose the word that fits the noun: much, many, or a word that works with both.
stages.tip: much + non-count noun; many + plural count noun.

stages.title: Determiner or pronoun?
stages.intro: The registry index needs to know which job each word is doing. Decide, then prove it.
stages.learned: If the word introduces a following noun, it is a determiner; if it stands alone for a whole noun phrase, it is a pronoun.

evidence: No noun follows; Those is the whole subject
It refers to something far away
items.why: Standing alone as a noun phrase: pronoun.

evidence: It is at the start of the sentence
items.why: It opens the noun phrase those registers.

evidence: yours is the independent possessive form, used without a noun

items.s: The forms are ready; [[each]] has a number.
evidence: No noun follows; each is the subject
items.why: Used alone as the subject: pronoun.

stages.task: Decide if the highlighted word is a determiner or a pronoun. Then choose the evidence.
stages.tip: Does a noun follow it?

stages.title: Check the certificates
stages.intro: Five certificates contain a determiner error. Find it and repair it.
stages.learned: Singular count nouns need a determiner; only one central determiner; an depends on sound.

items.s: The applicant is [[engineer]] at the power station.
items.task: A word is missing before one noun. Tap that noun.
items.why: A singular count noun needs a determiner; engineer begins with a vowel sound: an.

items.s: She studied at [[an]] university in Almaty.
[[The honesty]] is required of all officials.
items.why: A non-count abstract noun in a general statement takes no article.

items.s: There isn't [[many]] space in the archive.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

stages.title: Order the determiners
stages.intro: When determiners combine, their order is fixed: predeterminer, central determiner, postdeterminer. Rebuild each phrase.
stages.learned: Predeterminers (all, both, half) precede central determiners (the, my, these), which precede postdeterminers (numerals, other, many).
stages.task: Put the determiners in the correct order.
stages.tip: Example: all the other students.

CASES.title: Night at Central Station
CASES.brief:
Something happened on platform four between eleven and midnight, and the incident log is unreadable. The fault stripped the verbs of their forms and left out the words they need after them.

Verbs are the engine of every sentence. Rebuild the events in order, and we will know what happened.
CASES.debrief:
The night's events are clear. You found the verbs in the log, recognised what each verb needs after it, repaired tense forms, distinguished linking verbs from action verbs, and reconstructed complete clauses.

The station master's rule: learn a verb with its pattern, not just its meaning. put needs an object and a place.

stages.title: Read the incident log
stages.intro: Find every lexical verb (main verb) in the log. Auxiliaries are not targets; but when be is the only verb in its clause, it is the main verb. Some words that look like verbs are nouns.
stages.trap: Not a lexical verb here. Is it an auxiliary before another verb, or a noun after a determiner?
stages.learned: The lexical verb carries the main meaning; auxiliaries come before it; nouns like stop or call follow determiners.

items.text: At 23:10 a guard {heard} a noise near platform four. He {checked} the gate and {called} the control room. The call {was} short. A man was {standing} by the last carriage.

notes.checked: past tense with the object the gate.
notes.called: past tense with the object the control room.
notes.standing: the lexical verb of the progressive was standing.
notes.was: in The call was short, was is the only verb: a linking verb acting as the main verb.

traps.was: was is the progressive auxiliary here; the lexical verb is standing.

items.why: Five main verbs carried the action. call after The was a noun, and the second was was only an auxiliary.

stages.task: Find all the main (lexical) verbs in the log.
stages.tip: Do not choose auxiliaries. But when be is the only verb in its clause, choose it.

stages.title: What does the verb need?
stages.intro: Each verb in the log selects what must follow it. Sort the verbs by their pattern in the sentence shown.
stages.learned: Valency: intransitive verbs need nothing; transitive verbs need objects; linking verbs need a complement describing the subject.

items.ctx: The guard showed the inspector the tickets.
items.why: Indirect object the inspector, direct object the tickets.
Intransitive; in the office is an optional adverbial.

stages.task: Sort each verb by what must follow it in this sentence.

stages.title: Repair the timeline
stages.intro: Type the correct verb form. Check the subject, the time and any auxiliary.
stages.learned: Third person -s in the present; irregular pasts and participles are learned as vocabulary; after have the past participle, after be in the passive the past participle.

items.s: At 23:15 the guard ___ a torch from the office.

items.why: Passive: was + past participle; shut has the same form in all three.

items.s: The cameras ___ nothing unusual that night.

items.why: Irregular past: ring → rang; no did because who is the subject.

stages.task: Type the correct form of the verb.
stages.tip: Check the subject, the time and any auxiliary.

stages.title: Question the witness
stages.intro: A passenger describes what she noticed. Choose the reply that accurately reflects what she means. Linking verbs take adjectives; action verbs take adverbs.
stages.learned: After a linking verb, an adjective describes the subject; with an action verb, an adverb describes the action.

lines: The carriage smelled strange, like smoke.

options.t: So the smell in the carriage was strange.
options.why: smell is linking here: the carriage was strange in smell.

options.t: So you smelled strangely in the carriage.
options.reply: I beg your pardon? I didn't do anything strangely.
options.why: strangely would describe the manner of an action of smelling, which is not what she meant.

options.t: So the carriage had no smell at all.
options.why: She said it smelled strange: linking smell + adjective describes the carriage.

lines: The man looked carefully at the timetable.

options.t: So he studied it with care.
options.why: look at is an action here; carefully describes how.

options.t: So he seemed careful.
options.reply: I didn't say what he seemed like. I said how he looked at it.
options.why: The adverb describes the action, not the man.

options.t: So the timetable looked careful.
options.why: The adverb modifies looked, the man's action.

options.t: So he appeared calm after the incident.
options.why: look = appear: linking verb + adjective.

options.t: So he looked at something calmly.
options.reply: No, I meant how he seemed.
options.why: With an adjective, look is linking and describes the subject.

options.t: So he searched calmly.
options.why: calm (adjective) describes him, not an action.

stages.task: Choose the reply that matches what the passenger means.
stages.tip: Linking verbs take adjectives (She seemed calm). Action verbs take adverbs (She spoke calmly).

stages.title: Reconstruct the events
stages.intro: The final report was torn into pieces. Restore the sentences. Each verb needs its required elements.
stages.learned: Every clause follows its verb's pattern: put + object + place, give + two objects, become + complement.

a: The man put a bag on the bench
items.why: put requires an object and a place (SVOA).

a: The guard gave the driver a warning
items.why: Ditransitive: indirect object before direct object.
arrive takes no direct object: *arrived the station is impossible.

stages.task: Rebuild each sentence of the report.
stages.tip: Each verb needs its required elements.

CASES.title: The Interview Room
CASES.brief:
Interviews depend on questions, and English questions depend on auxiliaries. The fault deleted every do, did and does from our question sheets and mixed up the modal verbs.

Before the suspect from Central Station arrives, I need a clean set of questions and a clear sense of what must, might and should mean.
CASES.debrief:
The interview went well. You identified auxiliaries with the NICE tests, built questions with inversion and do-support, interpreted modal meanings, and corrected auxiliary errors.

Remember: in a question with a lexical verb, the tense moves to do/does/did, and the lexical verb returns to its base form.

stages.title: Auxiliary or lexical verb?
stages.intro: Decide whether the highlighted verb is an auxiliary or a lexical verb, then choose the evidence.
stages.learned: Auxiliaries come before another verb and pass the NICE tests; be, have, do can be either.

evidence: It is followed by the participle left, and inversion works: Has he left?
It is the only verb and means possession
do carries the negative and the past; answer is the lexical verb
It is the only verb, meaning 'completed'
It takes a bare infinitive and has no -s: *he musts

stages.task: Decide if the highlighted verb is an auxiliary or a lexical verb. Then choose the evidence.
stages.tip: Is another verb carrying the main meaning?

stages.title: Prepare the question sheet
stages.intro: Build each question. Some sentences include a decoy piece that would make the question ungrammatical.
stages.learned: Questions invert an auxiliary with the subject; with a lexical verb, add do/does/did and use the base form.

a: Where did you go on Tuesday ?
items.why: Past tense is carried by did; go stays in the base form.

a: Does your brother work at the station ?
Have you seen this man before ?
Why were you waiting on platform four ?
items.why: Progressive auxiliary were inverts with the subject.

stages.task: Build each question.
stages.tip: One piece may not belong. Leave it out.

stages.title: Reading the modals
stages.intro: During the interview, the precise modal matters. Choose the interpretation or reply that matches the modal used.
stages.learned: must can express obligation or near-certain deduction; might expresses possibility; should expresses advice or expectation.

lines: The bag must be in the left-luggage office.

options.t: He is almost certain it is there.
options.why: Epistemic must: a confident deduction.

options.t: He is ordering someone to put it there.
options.reply: I'm not ordering anyone. I'm saying where it probably is.
options.why: must be + location here is deduction, not obligation.

options.t: He has no idea where it is.
options.why: must expresses strong certainty.

lines: I might have seen him on the train.

options.t: He's not sure; it's a possibility.
options.why: might have + participle: past possibility.

options.t: He definitely saw him.
options.why: might is tentative.

options.t: He was allowed to see him.
options.reply: Allowed? No, I mean perhaps I saw him.
options.why: might here is possibility, not permission.

lines: Can I make a phone call?

options.t: Yes, you can call from the office next door.
options.why: can + bare infinitive for permission.

options.t: Yes, you can to call from the office.
options.why: No to after a modal.

options.t: Yes, you cans call from the office.
options.why: Modals take no -s.

lines: Will I be able to leave tonight?
items.prompt: Explain that it will be possible tomorrow, not tonight:

options.t: Not tonight, but you will be able to leave tomorrow.
options.why: Standard English does not combine two central modals; be able to works after will.

options.t: Not tonight, but you will can leave tomorrow.
options.why: *will can is impossible; use will be able to.

options.t: Not tonight, but you can will leave tomorrow.
options.why: Two modals cannot follow each other.

stages.task: Choose the reply that matches the modal verb.

stages.title: Check the transcript
stages.intro: The typist made auxiliary errors in the transcript. Find and repair each one.
stages.learned: Tense is marked once; modals take a bare infinitive and no -s; third person singular needs does.

items.s: Did you [[saw]] the man on the platform?

items.task: An auxiliary is missing before one word. Tap that word.
items.why: A question with a lexical verb needs did: Where did you put…?
Modals take the bare infinitive: should wait.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

CASES.title: The Gallery Forgery
CASES.brief:
Our new exhibition opens tomorrow, and someone has tampered with the wall labels. Descriptions now modify the wrong things: adverbs describe paintings, adjectives describe actions, and the word order is clumsy.

A forger leaves traces. Find out what each modifier really modifies, and the forged labels will expose themselves.
CASES.debrief:
The labels are authentic again. You identified adjectives with the very and seem tests, worked out what each modifier modifies, formed adverbs and comparatives, ordered adjectives naturally and placed adverbs correctly.

The curator's rule: adjectives modify nouns or describe the subject after a linking verb; adverbs modify everything else.

stages.title: Read the catalogue
stages.intro: Find every adjective in the catalogue entry. Nouns used as modifiers are not adjectives; test with very.
stages.trap: Not an adjective here. Try very in front, or check whether it modifies a verb.
stages.learned: Adjectives modify nouns or follow linking verbs; nouns as modifiers fail the very test; adverbs modify verbs and adjectives.

items.text: This {small} oil painting shows a {quiet} harbour at dawn. The colours are {soft} and {warm}, and the {old} fishing boats look almost {real}.

traps.oil: oil is a noun modifying painting: *a very oil painting.
traps.fishing: fishing classifies the boats by purpose; *very fishing boats is impossible.

items.why: Six adjectives. The traps were nouns and -ing forms used as classifying modifiers, and the adverb almost.

stages.task: Find all the adjectives in the catalogue entry.
stages.tip: Nouns used as modifiers are not adjectives. Test with very.

stages.title: What does it modify?
stages.intro: For each bold word on the labels, decide what it modifies.
stages.learned: Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs or whole clauses.

items.ctx: A bright sky fills the upper half.

items.why: A stance adverb commenting on the whole clause.

items.ctx: The light fades slowly towards the edges.
It is the gallery's most famous work.

items.why: The speaker's comment on the situation.

stages.task: Decide what the bold word modifies.

stages.title: Correct the labels
stages.intro: Type the word that fits each gap: an adjective, an adverb, or a comparative or superlative.
stages.learned: Use -ly adverbs for manner (with exceptions like well, fast, hard); one syllable takes -er/-est; long adjectives take more/most.

items.s: The artist painted very ___ in her later years.
This is the ___ painting in the collection.
Her early work is ___ than her late work.
items.hint: Long adjectives use a separate word.

items.why: A degree adverb modifying the adjective disappointed.

items.s: The gallery is ___ than the museum.

stages.task: Type the word that fits the gap.
stages.tip: You may need an adjective, an adverb, or a comparative or superlative.

stages.title: Rewrite the forged descriptions
stages.intro: The forger scrambled the word order. Rebuild each label so the adjectives follow their usual order and the adverbs sit in natural positions.
stages.learned: Opinion before size, age, colour, origin and material; frequency adverbs before the main verb; never between a verb and its object.

a: The artist often painted the sea
items.why: Frequency adverb in mid position, before the main verb.
Manner adverb after the object, not between verb and object.

stages.task: Rebuild each label in natural word order.
stages.tip: Adjectives usually go opinion, size, age, colour, origin, material.

stages.title: Expose the forged labels
stages.intro: Each label contains one modifier error that a curator would never make. Find it and repair it.
stages.learned: Non-gradable adjectives reject very; predicative-only adjectives cannot precede a noun; linking verbs take adjectives.

items.s: A [[very]] unique portrait of the artist's mother.
The [[asleep]] child in the corner is the artist's son.
items.why: asleep is predicative-only: the child is asleep, but the sleeping child.

items.s: The painting looks [[beautifully]] in the new light.
The gallery [[hardly works]] to protect its collection.
items.why: hardly means 'almost not'; the intended meaning is works hard.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

CASES.title: The Stopped Clocks
CASES.brief:
Every clock in the Clockworks has stopped. The misprint scrambled the adverbs on my repair cards: they no longer say how, when, how often or how much, and some adverbs sit in the wrong place.

Find the adverbs, sort them by meaning, repair their forms and positions, and the clocks will tick again.
CASES.debrief:
The clocks are ticking again. You found adverbs among -ly adjectives, sorted them by meaning, chose between flat adverbs and their -ly partners, and put each adverb in its natural position.

The clockmaker's rule: ask what the word modifies. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs and whole clauses, but not nouns.

stages.title: Read the repair log
stages.intro: Find every adverb in the clockmaker's log. The -ly ending is a clue, not a proof.
stages.trap: Not an adverb here. Ask what the word modifies: a noun means an adjective.
stages.learned: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs and whole clauses; friendly and lonely are adjectives despite -ly; late and hard can be adverbs without -ly.

items.text: The tower clock {usually} strikes {loudly} at noon. {Yesterday} it struck {twice}, {very} {quietly}, and {then} stopped {completely}. Its friendly keeper looked lonely and worked {late} into the night.

notes.completely: degree: to what extent it stopped.
notes.late: a flat adverb: worked late. lately would mean 'recently'.

traps.friendly: an adjective ending in -ly: it modifies the noun keeper.
traps.lonely: an adjective after the linking verb looked.

items.why: Nine adverbs. The traps friendly and lonely are adjectives: the -ly ending is a clue, not a proof.

stages.title: Sort the repair cards
stages.intro: Each card names one adverb. Decide which question it answers: how? when or where? how often? to what extent? Or is it the speaker's comment?
stages.learned: Manner answers how?, time and place when? and where?, frequency how often?, degree to what extent?; stance adverbs comment on the whole clause.

items.why: The speaker's comment on the whole clause, in front position.

items.ctx: Sadly, the oldest clock cannot be saved.
items.why: The speaker's feeling about the whole situation.

items.ctx: The clockmaker always checks the time twice.

stages.title: Repair the forms
stages.intro: Type the adverb that fits each gap. Some adverbs have no -ly, and some -ly forms mean something different.
stages.learned: Flat adverbs: hard, late, fast, high; different meanings: hardly (almost not), lately (recently), highly (very); well → better, fast → faster.

items.s: I can ___ hear the ticking; the room is so noisy.

items.why: How to handle it: manner adverb with -ly.

items.s: The new clock runs ___ than the old one.
items.why: fast is a flat adverb: comparative faster, not *more fastly.

items.s: She repaired it ___ than anyone else.
items.why: The adverb is well; its comparative is better.

stages.title: Put the adverbs back
stages.intro: The misprint moved the adverbs. Rebuild each sentence with every adverb in a natural position.
stages.learned: Frequency adverbs go in mid position: before the main verb, after the first auxiliary and after be; manner adverbs usually go at the end; never between a verb and its object.

a: She has never repaired a clock like this
items.why: Mid position: after the first auxiliary has.
Manner adverb at the end or before the verb, but not between wound and its object.

a: We often work late on Fridays
items.why: Frequency adverb before the main verb; late (time) at the end.
The degree adverb extremely comes directly before the adverb it modifies.

stages.title: Find the faulty cards
stages.intro: Each card has one adverb error. Find it and choose the repair.
stages.learned: Do not separate a verb from its object; frequency adverbs follow be; friendly has no adverb form; well is the adverb of good; late and lately differ in meaning.

items.why: Do not separate the verb from its object: repaired the clock carefully.
It describes how the clock works: the adverb well.

items.s: The keeper smiled [[friendlily]] at the visitors.
items.why: friendly is an adjective with no adverb form: in a friendly way.

items.s: The bus was delayed, so we arrived [[lately]].

CASES.title: The Map Room
CASES.brief:
The fault scrambled the descriptions in our street directory. Couriers are getting lost because opposite became next to, and in became on.

Go into the field with the plan. Read each message, find the place it describes, and then help me repair the directory and the phrasal verbs our staff keep misusing.
CASES.debrief:
The directory is reliable again. You interpreted spatial prepositions on a real plan, distinguished prepositions from particles, chose the prepositions that verbs and adjectives select, and corrected particle placement.

The cartographer's rule: a preposition relates a noun phrase to the rest of the sentence; a particle belongs to its verb and can move after the object.

stages.title: Find the deliveries
stages.intro: Each courier message describes one building. Read the prepositions carefully and tap the right place on the plan.
stages.learned: opposite = facing across a road; between = with one on each side; next to = beside; on the corner of = where two roads meet.

deco: <text x="368" y="230" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="var(--ink3)" transform="rotate(-90 368 230)" letter-spacing="1">PARK LANE</text>

items.instr: The parcel goes to the building between the bank and Park Lane, on Main Street.
items.why: Between the bank (left) and Park Lane (right) on the north side of Main Street: the café.

items.instr: Deliver it to the building opposite the café, across Main Street.
items.why: opposite = facing it on the other side of the road: the post office.

items.instr: It's on River Road, opposite the pharmacy.
items.why: Across River Road from the pharmacy: the station.

items.instr: The flowers are for the building next to the park, opposite the hotel.
items.why: Beside the park and facing the hotel across Main Street: the museum.

items.instr: Leave the box at the building on the corner of Main Street and Park Lane, on the right of the lane, facing the park.
items.why: North side of Main Street, on the right of Park Lane, across from the park: the library.

items.instr: It's on River Road, between the school and the gym.
items.why: With the school on one side and the gym on the other: the bakery.

items.instr: The keys are in the building opposite the station, on the other side of River Road.
items.why: Facing the station across River Road: the pharmacy.

stages.task: Read the message. Tap the building it describes on the map.
stages.tip: The prepositions tell you where to go.

stages.title: Preposition or particle?
stages.intro: Directory entries use small words like up, off, in. Decide whether each bold word is a preposition (with a noun phrase after it) or a particle belonging to the verb. Try moving it after the object.
stages.learned: A particle can follow a noun object and must follow a pronoun object (turn it off); a preposition stays before its noun phrase (look at it).

items.why: up the hill is a place phrase; *ran the hill up is impossible.

items.ctx: Please pick up the parcel at nine.
items.why: pick the parcel up is possible: phrasal verb.
turn the engine off / turn it off.
off the van: movement away from a place.
fill the form in / fill it in.
Prepositional verb: *look the map at is impossible.
write the address down / write it down.

stages.task: Decide if the bold word is a preposition or a particle.
stages.tip: Try moving it after the object. If you can, it is a particle.

stages.title: Repair the directory phrases
stages.intro: Each phrase needs the preposition that its verb, adjective or noun selects. Choose from the chips or type it.
stages.learned: Dependent prepositions are selected by the word before them and must be learned with it.

items.s: The driver is responsible ___ the vehicle.
We arrived ___ the airport at six.
items.why: arrive at a point (arrive in a city or country); never *arrive to.

stages.task: Type or choose the preposition that completes the phrase.

stages.title: Correct the staff notes
stages.intro: The staff notes contain preposition and particle errors. Find each and repair it.
stages.learned: Some verbs take a direct object with no preposition; particles follow pronoun objects; dependent prepositions are fixed.

items.s: The radio is too loud; please [[turn down it]].
items.why: With a pronoun object, the particle follows it: turn it down.

items.s: She entered [[into]] the building at noon.
items.why: enter a place takes a direct object.

items.s: He is married [[with]] the station manager.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

CASES.title: The Torn Diary
CASES.brief:
A diary donated to the archive was damaged in the fault. The sentences survived, but every word that joined them disappeared. Without the links we cannot tell cause from contrast, or which event happened first.

Restore the connections, then help me prepare a phone call to the donor's family without sounding like a textbook.
CASES.debrief:
The diary reads as one story again. You restored coordinators and subordinators according to meaning, separated conjunctions from linking adverbs such as however, removed doubled links, and used inserts appropriately in conversation.

The archivist's rule: one relationship, one link. Although or but, never both.

stages.title: Restore the links
stages.intro: Choose the connecting word that restores the meaning of each diary entry.
stages.learned: because = reason, so = result, but and although = contrast, when, until, before = time, unless = negative condition.

items.s: We stayed indoors ___ the storm was too strong.
The storm was too strong, ___ we stayed indoors.
___ it was late, my father kept writing.
items.why: Contrast between being late and continuing: Although.

items.s: We waited at the pier ___ the boat arrived.
items.why: Waiting continues up to the time of arrival: until.

items.s: You can't sail ___ you have a licence.
items.why: unless = if not: sailing is allowed only with a licence.

items.s: I wanted to write more, ___ the candle went out.
items.why: Contrast between two equal clauses: the coordinator but.

stages.task: Choose the linking word that restores the meaning.

stages.title: Classify the linking words
stages.intro: The archive index needs the class of each linking word. Use the clue: could the clause stand alone, and how is the word punctuated?
stages.learned: Coordinators join equals; subordinators make a dependent clause; linking adverbs begin a new sentence or follow a semicolon; inserts stand outside the clause.

items.ctx: We left early because it was dark.
items.why: because it was dark cannot stand alone.

items.ctx: The house was cold. However, nobody complained.
items.why: It begins a new sentence and is followed by a comma.

items.ctx: My mother cooked and my father read aloud.

items.why: A discourse marker outside the clause.

items.ctx: Although we were poor, we were happy.
items.why: Introduces a dependent clause of contrast.

items.ctx: The road was closed; therefore, we walked.
items.why: After a semicolon and followed by a comma: an adverb.

items.ctx: We could take the bus or walk.

stages.task: Decide the class of each linking word.
stages.tip: Could the clause stand alone? Look at the punctuation too.

stages.title: The transcriber's errors
stages.intro: A transcriber typed the diary but doubled some links and misused others. Find each error and repair it.
stages.learned: Use one link per relationship; however cannot join two clauses with a comma; correlatives come in fixed pairs.

items.s: Although we had little money, [[but]] we travelled every summer.
Because the bridge was closed, [[so]] we took the ferry.
The ferry was late, [[however]] we caught the train.
items.why: however is an adverb and cannot join two clauses with a comma; but can.

items.s: Neither my brother [[or]] my sister wrote back.
Either we leave now [[nor]] we miss the last ferry.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

stages.title: The phone call
stages.intro: You call the donor's granddaughter, Aruzhan. Inserts such as well, oh and sorry, and stance adverbs such as actually, manage the conversation. Choose natural replies.
stages.learned: Inserts do social work: softening, correcting, reacting, apologising. They belong to speech, not to formal writing.

options.t: Hi, this is Timur from the City Archive. Is this a good time?
options.reply: Yes, of course. How can I help?
options.why: Greeting + a polite check: natural opening.

options.t: The diary. Bring information.
options.reply: Sorry? I'm not sure who this is.
options.why: No greeting, no context: the call feels abrupt and unclear.

options.t: Dear Madam, I am writing to inform you…
options.why: Formal written formulae are out of place in speech.

lines: So the diary was completely destroyed?
items.prompt: Correct her politely: it is damaged, not destroyed.

options.t: Actually, it's only damaged. We can still read most of it.
options.why: Actually signals a polite correction.

options.t: No. Wrong.
options.why: Accurate, but too blunt: nothing softens the correction.

options.t: Yeah, totally destroyed, but also we can read it.
options.reply: I'm confused. Is it destroyed or not?
options.why: Agreeing first contradicts the correction.

lines: Could you send me a copy of the pages you've restored?
items.prompt: Agree, and promise to send them tomorrow:

options.t: Sure, I'll send them tomorrow.
options.why: A response form (Sure) followed by a clear promise.

options.t: Um, er, well, yes, um.
options.why: Hesitators hold the turn, but too many leave the message unclear.

options.t: Well, actually, anyway.
options.why: Discourse words alone carry no message.

stages.task: Choose the most natural reply.
stages.tip: Small words like well, actually and oh manage the conversation.

CASES.title: The Laboratory Notebook
CASES.brief:
My laboratory studies how forms change their jobs. The fault damaged our notebook exactly where verbs become non-finite: -ing forms, infinitives, and adjectives made from participles.

One -ing form can do several jobs. Your task is to identify the job each time, then repair the notebook.
CASES.debrief:
The notebook is restored. You classified -ing forms by their function, chose between -ing and to-infinitive after verbs, distinguished feeling-causing -ing adjectives from feeling-experiencing -ed adjectives, and justified your analyses with evidence.

The laboratory's principle: ask what job a form is doing, not what it is called.

stages.title: Sample analysis
stages.intro: Each sample contains an -ing form. Sort it by the job it does in its sentence.
stages.learned: The -ing form appears in progressive verb phrases, in noun-phrase positions, as a modifier, and in adverbial clauses.

items.why: It heads the subject, but it also takes an object (each sample), a verbal property.

items.ctx: The students are testing the samples now.

items.why: It describes the results after were; the results seemed amazing and amazing results are both possible: an adjective.

items.ctx: Looking at the data again, she saw the error.
items.why: A participle clause giving the circumstances of she saw.
A participial modifier before a noun meaning 'that works'.
After the preposition at, in a noun-phrase position.

stages.task: Decide what job the -ing form does in its sentence.

stages.title: Repair the procedure
stages.intro: The procedure lost its verb forms. Type -ing or to + verb, as the main verb requires.
stages.learned: The verb decides: enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest + -ing; decide, plan, refuse, hope + to; remember, stop, try change meaning.

items.s: Avoid ___ the samples with bare hands.
Remember ___ the lid before you leave.
I remember ___ that machine for the first time in 2019.
We look forward to ___ the results.
items.why: to is a preposition here, so -ing follows.
items.hint: Is to part of an infinitive, or a preposition?

items.s: He stopped ___ a sandwich and then continued.
items.why: stop to do = stop in order to do something.

stages.task: Type the verb as -ing or to + verb.
stages.tip: The verb before the gap decides.

stages.title: Feedback from volunteers
stages.intro: Volunteers describe how they felt during the study. Choose the reply that understands them correctly.
stages.learned: -ing adjectives describe the cause of a feeling; -ed adjectives describe the person who feels it.

lines: Honestly, I was bored after the first hour.

options.t: Sorry the session felt so long. We'll add a break.
options.why: bored = how she felt; you respond to her feeling.

options.t: I don't think you're boring at all!
options.reply: I didn't say I was boring. I said I was bored!
options.why: boring would describe her as the cause of boredom.

options.t: So you made the others bored?
options.why: -ed describes the experiencer, not the cause.

lines: The last task was really confusing.

options.t: Thanks, we'll rewrite the instructions.
options.why: confusing describes the task as the cause.

options.t: Don't worry, many people are confusing.
options.reply: I meant the task, not people!
options.why: confusing people cause confusion; the volunteer meant the task.

options.t: So you confused the task?
options.why: The task caused the confusion.

lines: I'm really interested in the results.

options.t: We'll email you a summary.
options.why: interested = the volunteer's feeling.

options.t: Yes, you're a very interesting person.
options.reply: Thank you, but that's not what I said.
options.why: interesting would describe the volunteer as causing interest.

options.t: Interested results are rare.
options.why: Only people (experiencers) can be interested.

stages.task: Choose the reply that understands the volunteer.
stages.tip: -ing describes the cause (boring); -ed describes the feeling (bored).

stages.title: Peer review
stages.intro: A reviewer questioned four analyses. Decide the classification and select the evidence that answers the reviewer.
stages.learned: Adjectival -ing/-ed forms accept very and seem; verbal ones take objects and appear in progressive or passive constructions.

evidence: The results seemed very disappointing is natural
items.why: Adjective tests succeed; it has no object.

items.s: The delays were [[disappointing]] the sponsors more every week.
items.why: An object shows a verb: progressive were disappointing the sponsors.

evidence: It follows the linking verb looked, which cannot form a passive
items.why: After a linking verb, the participle describes a state: an adjective.

items.s: The window was [[broken]] by a stone last night.
evidence: The by-phrase names an agent and last night dates an event
items.why: An agent and a time adverbial make it a passive event.

stages.task: Choose the class of the highlighted word. Then choose the evidence.

CASES.title: The Word Workshop
CASES.brief:
This is where the fault began. Our typesetting machine builds words from roots and affixes, and it started producing the wrong members of each word family: verbs where nouns belong, adjectives where adverbs belong.

Work the bench with me. Build the right form for each slot, recognise when a word has changed class without changing shape, and check the machine's output.
CASES.debrief:
The machine is repaired. You built nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs from shared roots, used suffixes as evidence of class, recognised conversion and its stress patterns, and corrected word-family errors.

The workshop rule: decide which class the slot needs first, then choose the form.

stages.title: Build the family member
stages.intro: Each slot needs one member of the word family. Decide the class the position requires, then type the form.
stages.learned: Position decides the class; suffixes such as -tion, -ive, -en, -ly deliver it.

items.s: The ___ of the new press took six months.

items.why: After a genitive determiner: a noun (-ity).
After to, with an object: a verb (-en).
Between very and a noun: an adjective (-ive).

items.s: The new design is a great ___ .
Please ___ the instructions for new staff.
The staff were ___ about the changes.
items.why: After the linking verb were: an adjective (-ic).

stages.task: Type the member of the word family that fits the gap.
stages.tip: First decide which class the position needs.

stages.title: Sort the suffixes
stages.intro: Each piece of type shows a word made with a suffix. Which class does the suffix usually create?
stages.learned: Suffixes are strong clues to class, though not absolute proof (friendly is an adjective).

items.why: -ly on a noun forms an adjective: a friendly person. On adjectives it forms adverbs.

stages.task: Decide which class each suffix usually makes.

stages.title: Same shape, new class
stages.intro: Conversion changes class without changing form. Decide the class in each sentence and identify the evidence.
stages.learned: In conversion, position and form tests decide; in some noun–verb pairs stress moves (REcord / reCORD).

items.s: Please [[email]] the proofs to the editor.
evidence: Imperative position with an object, the proofs; it can become emailed
After the modal will; in speech, stress on the second syllable: reCORD
After the; in speech, stress on the first syllable: REcord
items.why: Noun, stressed on the first syllable.

evidence: After Let's, with an object; it can become emptied

stages.task: Choose the class of the highlighted word. Then choose the evidence.
stages.tip: Same form, different class: look at its position.

stages.title: Check the machine's output
stages.intro: The machine still slips into the wrong family member. Find each faulty word and choose the repair.
stages.learned: The most persistent word-form errors involve the wrong member of a known family; check position first.

items.s: The [[decide]] to close the plant was unpopular.
The new press is far more [[efficiency]] than the old one.
items.why: After more and a linking verb: adjective.

items.s: The workshop has a long and [[success]] history.
items.why: Coordinated with long before a noun: adjective.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

CASES.title: The Blueprint Office
CASES.brief:
Every sentence in this city is built on a blueprint: subject, verb, object, complement, adverbial. The fault scrambled the labels on our plans, and some clauses were rebuilt in the wrong order.

Label the blueprints, decide what the verb really needs, and rebuild the clauses so they stand.
CASES.debrief:
The blueprints are correct again. You labelled clause elements by function, separated obligatory complements from optional adjuncts, rebuilt the seven basic clause patterns, and repaired word order that had been transferred from verb-final languages.

The planner's rule: the verb decides what the clause needs; the rest is decoration.

stages.title: Label the blueprints
stages.intro: Each clause is divided into its elements. Tap each part to cycle through the labels until every element has its function.
stages.learned: Function is about the job in the clause: the same noun phrase can be subject, object or complement.

items.why: SVO: the bridge is what was checked.
SVC: safe describes the subject after the linking verb.
SVOO: indirect object the team, direct object a medal.

stages.task: Tap each part until it shows its function: S, V, O, C or A. Then press Check.

stages.title: Needed or optional?
stages.intro: The highlighted part follows the verb. Would the clause still be complete without it? Sort it.
stages.learned: Complements are selected by the verb and cannot be omitted without changing the meaning or grammar; adjuncts can be removed.

items.ctx: She put the file on the shelf.
The office is in the city centre.

items.why: The engineer lives is incomplete in this meaning: live needs a place.

stages.task: Decide if the highlighted part is needed or optional.
stages.tip: Remove it. Is the sentence still complete?

stages.title: Rebuild the clauses
stages.intro: The plan pieces are scattered, and one piece does not belong. Rebuild each clause in standard order.
stages.learned: English keeps the order Subject–Verb–Object; adverbials of place usually come before adverbials of time.

items.ctx: SVC: the complement describes the park.
items.why: After the linking verb looks, an adjective, not an adverb.

a: They sent the residents a letter
items.why: Indirect object before direct object, without to.

a: We met at the office on Monday
items.why: Place, then time is the usual order.

stages.task: Rebuild each clause in English word order.
stages.tip: One piece does not belong. Leave it out.

stages.title: Transferred word order
stages.intro: Some blueprints were drafted by a team used to verb-final languages such as Kazakh, or to the freer word order of Russian. Find the misplaced element and repair it.
stages.learned: In English the verb comes before its object, the object is not separated from its verb by an adverbial, and the subject is not dropped.

items.why: English is SVO: the verb comes before the object.
Do not separate the verb from its object: speaks English very well.
English requires a subject, even the dummy it.
Use SVOO without to, or put to her after the object: the plans to her.
Keep the object next to its verb: I like this city very much.

stages.task: Tap the misplaced words. Then choose the correct order.

CASES.title: The Ledger Goes to Press

who.name: Director Ines Kerey
who.role: Records Office, with the Ledger's editor

CASES.brief:
Every district is restored. Tonight the Meridian Ledger prints the full story of the fault, and the editor wants every word checked before the presses run.

This final case combines everything you have learned. Words change class from sentence to sentence; you will need all the tests at once.
CASES.debrief:
The Ledger is printed. You classified the hardest words in English, those that move between classes, by their position, form and function, and you justified each decision with evidence.

You can now do what the Bureau does: look at any word in any sentence and explain what it is doing there.

stages.title: The shape-shifters
stages.intro: The same word appears in different jobs. Decide its class in each sentence and choose the evidence.
stages.learned: Words such as round, that, since, before belong to several classes; only the sentence decides.

evidence: After the linking verb is, describing the subject; very round works
It takes the noun phrase the lake as its complement
After the determiner the and the modifier first; it can be plural: rounds

items.s: I think [[that]] the report is accurate.
evidence: It introduces a whole clause and can be omitted: I think the report is accurate
It stands alone as the subject; no noun follows
It is followed by a noun phrase, not a clause

items.s: [[Since]] the bridge was closed, we took the ferry.
evidence: It is followed by a full clause with a verb, the bridge was closed
items.why: Subordinator of reason, as in Quirk et al. (1985), the framework of this course. The last stage shows how the Cambridge Grammar analyses such words.

stages.task: Choose the class of the highlighted word. Then choose the evidence.

stages.title: Proofread the headline story
stages.intro: The editor wants every noun in the lead paragraph marked for the index. Watch for words that are nouns in one place and verbs or adjectives in another.
stages.trap: Not a noun here. Check the position: does it follow a determiner, or does it act as a verb or modifier?
stages.learned: Conversion means that form alone cannot decide class; a determiner or a noun-phrase position is the strongest evidence.

items.text: The {city} will record the {damage} in a new {report}. {Engineers} record every {crack}, and their {work} will help {residents} who work near the {river}.

traps.record: after will or after a plural subject: a verb.

items.why: record was a verb both times. work was a noun after their and a verb after who.

stages.task: Find all the nouns in the story.
stages.tip: Some words are nouns in one place and verbs in another.

stages.title: Final corrections
stages.intro: The last proof has errors from every district. Find each one and choose the repair.
stages.learned: Each error belongs to one word class; identifying the class is the first step to the repair.

items.s: The city gave us a lot of [[informations]] about the fault.

items.why: Describes how the repairs were done: adverb.
Every + singular noun takes a singular verb.

items.s: The engineers are interested [[for]] the results.
[[Despite of]] the storm, the presses ran on time.
The mayor thanked the workers and [[gave to them]] a medal.

stages.task: Tap the wrong word. Then choose the correction.

stages.title: The final blueprint
stages.intro: Label the clauses of the Ledger's closing paragraph.
stages.learned: Clause functions and word classes are two separate layers: a noun phrase can be S, O or C; an adverbial can be an adverb, a prepositional phrase, or a noun phrase.

items.why: Last night is a noun phrase functioning as an adverbial.
became is a linking verb; the noun phrase is a complement.

stages.task: Tap each part until it shows its function: S, V, O, C or A. Then press Check.

stages.title: The editor's borderline cases
stages.intro: The editor kept the hardest questions for last. Grammars do not all agree on these; choose the analysis the evidence best supports, following the Cambridge Grammar of the English Language (Huddleston & Pullum, 2002). Elsewhere this course follows Quirk et al. (1985).
stages.learned: Modern grammars treat many traditional 'subordinating conjunctions' as prepositions taking clauses, and many determiners as a separate function from the word class.

evidence: The same word takes a noun phrase (before the speeches) with the same meaning, so it can be treated as one preposition taking different complements
items.why: Huddleston & Pullum (2002) treat before, after and since as prepositions with noun-phrase or clause complements. Traditional grammars call this use a conjunction; both analyses are found in teaching materials.

evidence: It takes a complement, like a preposition, and does not accept very: very worth is odd
items.why: worth is a notoriously difficult word. Huddleston & Pullum (2002) classify it as a preposition; many dictionaries list it as an adjective.

evidence: It cannot be plural (the poors) and still accepts very: the very poor
items.why: An adjective heading a noun phrase with a plural meaning, not a converted noun.

stages.task: Choose the analysis that the evidence supports best.
stages.tip: These questions follow the Cambridge Grammar (Huddleston & Pullum, 2002).

lede.en: Sources cited in the explanations, in APA 7 format. Grammatical descriptions follow the reference grammars; teaching design follows the research on instructed second language acquisition and learning science.
lede.kk: Түсіндірмелерде сілтеме жасалған дереккөздер (APA 7 форматы). Грамматикалық сипаттамалар анықтамалық грамматикаларға, ал оқыту құрылымы екінші тілді меңгеру мен оқу ғылымы саласындағы зерттеулерге сүйенеді.
lede.ru: Источники, цитируемые в объяснениях, в формате APA 7. Грамматические описания следуют справочным грамматикам, а построение обучения — исследованиям в области обучения второму языку и наук об обучении.

hunt.name: Word hunt
steps: Read the document.
Tap every {target} you find.
Find them all to finish. A wrong tap shows you why.

sort.name: Sort the cards
steps: Read the word and its sentence.
Tap the box it belongs in, or drag the card there.
Sort every card to finish.

forge.name: Fill the gap
steps: Read the sentence.
Type the missing word, or tap a suggestion. Then press Check.
Fill every gap to finish.

fault.name: Find the error
steps: Read the sentence. One part is wrong.
Tap the wrong part. Then choose the correction.
Fix every sentence to finish.

deduce.name: Prove it
steps: Look at the highlighted word.
Choose its class. Then choose the evidence that proves it.
Answer both parts for every sentence.

dialogue.name: Conversation
steps: Read what the person says.
Tap the best reply.
Reach the end of every conversation.

rebuild.name: Rebuild
steps: Read the clue.
Tap the pieces in order. Tap a placed piece to send it back. Then press Check.
Rebuild every sentence. Some have one extra piece.

map.name: Deliveries
steps: Read the message.
Tap the building it describes on the map.
Deliver every message.

link.name: Who is it?
steps: Find the highlighted pronoun.
Tap the words it refers to.
Trace every pronoun.

slots.name: Label the parts
steps: The sentence is split into parts.
Tap a part to change its label. Then press Check.
Label every sentence.

GAME_INTRO: Last night the great printing press of Meridian misfired. Words were blown out of their sentences and scattered across every island of the world. The Bureau of Language Records has sent Dexter, Spark, Luna and Aizere into the field, and you are joining them. Each quest takes the team to one island, where one part of speech has gone wrong. The final quest brings everything together on the front page of the city's newspaper.
GAME_DOSSIER:
← City map
The Meridian Bureau

Design dossier

The research basis, the game architecture and the reasoning behind every mechanic. The game was designed in this order: evidence first, mechanics second, content third, code last.

1. What the research says

Games can work, but the design decides. Meta-analyses find that well-designed digital games improve learning compared with conventional instruction, and that design features matter more than the label "game" (Clark et al., 2016; Wouters et al., 2013). Wouters et al. (2013) found serious games more effective for learning and retention, but not more motivating than conventional instruction, and more effective when combined with other instruction and played over several sessions. Mayer (2019) argues for a value-added approach: rather than asking whether games beat lessons, ask which features improve learning. In his review, explanatory feedback, self-explanation and pre-training add value, while elaborate narrative and decoration often do not.

Gamification is not game-based learning. Gamification adds game elements such as points, badges and leaderboards to a non-game activity (Deterding et al., 2011); game-based learning makes the activity itself the game (Plass et al., 2015). The gamification meta-analysis by Sailer and Homner (2020) found small positive effects, with the cognitive effect the most stable; tangible expected rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation (Deci et al., 1999). This is why the Bureau has no points, badges or leaderboards.

Motivation comes from competence, autonomy and relatedness. Self-Determination Theory explains game enjoyment through these three needs (Ryan & Deci, 2000; Ryan et al., 2006). Flow requires a balance between challenge and skill and clear goals with immediate feedback (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990). Malone (1981) identified challenge, curiosity and fantasy as sources of intrinsic motivation in instructional games, adding that the fantasy should be connected to the skill being learned.

Learning science constrains the design. Working memory is limited, so new content must not compete with complex game rules (Sweller, 1988). Retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving of confusable categories improve retention (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006; Nakata & Suzuki, 2019). Mastery learning requires learners to reach a criterion before moving on, with corrective loops for errors (Bloom, 1968). Experiential, situated and constructivist accounts stress learning through action in meaningful contexts (Kolb, 1984; Lave & Wenger, 1991).

2. From theory to mechanics

PrincipleSourceHow the Bureau applies it
Explanatory feedbackHattie & Timperley (2007); Mayer (2019)Every answer is evaluated immediately and explained grammatically, including wrong clicks in evidence hunts.
Mastery and corrective loopsBloom (1968)A wrongly answered item returns at the end of the stage; a stage closes only when every item is solved.
Challenge–skill balanceCsikszentmihalyi (1990)Each case escalates from recognition to distinction to application; stages are labelled with CEFR ranges.
Competence and autonomyRyan et al. (2006)Visible progress through real completion; every case is open, the map recommends the next one, and completed stages can be replayed in any order.
Cognitive loadSweller (1988)One mechanic per stage, a single new rule at a time, short sentences when the grammar is new.
Retrieval and interleavingRoediger & Karpicke (2006); Nakata & Suzuki (2019)Later cases reuse earlier classes; the final case mixes all of them.
Situated learning and endogenous fantasyLave & Wenger (1991); Malone (1981)Every task is a job the city needs: a lost-property report, a timetable, a map, a newspaper page. The grammar decision is the action.
Limited value of decorationMayer (2019)Narrative frames each case in a few sentences and never delays the task; sound and confetti are brief and can be muted.

DuolingoShort sessions, immediate feedback, regular practice. A semester-long study found that learning gains varied widely between learners and were related to the time they spent in the app (Loewen et al., 2019).Limited explanation of grammar; extrinsic streak mechanics. The Bureau links each case to a full explanation.
Kahoot!Fast feedback and high engagement in class; a review of 93 studies reported positive effects on performance and attitudes (Wang & Tahir, 2020).Time pressure and a quiz format that rewards speed. The Bureau is untimed.
WordwallVariety of templates for teacher-made tasks.Templates rather than designed progression. Each Bureau case is authored as a sequence.
Minecraft EducationExploration and construction in a shared world.Grammar has to be imposed on the world. In the Bureau the world is made of texts, so the grammar is the world.
The SimsEveryday situations and social interaction.No explicit language focus. The Bureau adapts the everyday-situation idea for its dialogues.
Educational escape roomsLinked puzzles, a goal and teamwork; a systematic review found strong engagement but few rigorous outcome studies (Veldkamp et al., 2020).Puzzles can become unrelated to the learning goal. Every Bureau puzzle is a grammar decision.
Mystery and adventure gamesCuriosity, clues and deduction.Long narrative passages delay the task. Bureau briefings are short.

No visual design, character or text from these products has been reproduced; only general design principles have been adapted.

5. Architecture

Concept. A connected investigation in one city. Thirteen cases follow the order of the explanation units, so each case reinforces what the learner has just studied. The city map is a single route: progress is literally a journey through the parts of speech.

Inside a case. A short briefing from a character sets a goal. Four or five stages follow, each with a different mechanic and a rising level: recognition, then distinction, then application, then a final stage that combines the case with earlier knowledge. Each stage ends by stating the principle the learner has established. The case debrief summarises the grammar and reports first-attempt accuracy, the only score shown, because it is the useful one.

Adaptation. Difficulty adapts through the mastery loop: items answered wrongly return until solved, so a learner who struggles gets more practice, and one who succeeds moves on quickly. Clues are available on request in the workbench stages. Accuracy below 60% in a case triggers a recommendation to re-read the unit and replay.

Levels. Early cases use short sentences and everyday vocabulary (A1–B1). Middle cases add distinctions and production (B1–B2). The last cases require analysis of ambiguity, competing frameworks and multiple simultaneous errors (C1–C2). Difficulty comes from the grammar, not from rare vocabulary.

Integration. Each explanation unit links to its case, and each case links back to its unit. Progress is saved on the learner's device.
